slides.title: Device Placement
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Secure architecture depends on where devices are placed, which trust zones they belong to, how they connect, what attack surface they expose, and what happens when a component fails.
course.why: Architecture determines the paths an attacker can use and the blast radius of each failure.
course.example: A public web server is placed in a DMZ, management interfaces are reachable only from an admin network, and firewalls fail closed where confidentiality is more important than continued access.
course.exam: Think trust boundaries, DMZ, segmentation, exposed interfaces, redundant paths, and fail-open versus fail-closed.

breakdown.explanation: Physical security protects people, buildings, devices, documents, and infrastructure from unauthorized physical access, theft, tampering, or environmental harm.

course.learn: Infrastructure devices have attributes that affect how they should be secured: active versus passive role, inline versus monitoring placement, update capability, management access, high-availability requirements, and traffic-analysis function.
course.why: Placement and function determine both the device's security value and the impact if it fails or is compromised.
course.example: An inline IPS can block attacks but may become a traffic bottleneck or outage point, while a passive tap observes traffic without sitting in the forwarding path.
course.exam: Inline can enforce/block; passive/tap observes. Management interfaces should be restricted and monitored.

defs: Port-based network access control that authenticates users/devices before allowing access to the network.

course.learn: Port security restricts who or what may use a network switch port. 802.1X is a common port-based access-control method that authenticates a user or device before normal network access is granted.
course.why: Physical access to an Ethernet jack should not automatically provide trusted network access.
course.example: A laptop connects to a switch, completes 802.1X authentication using EAP/RADIUS, and is assigned the appropriate network access.
course.exam: 802.1X = port-based NAC/authentication. EAP carries authentication methods; RADIUS commonly provides AAA services.

slides.teach: Focus on the differences between the listed types and the clue words that distinguish them in exam questions.
defs: A control that permits or blocks network traffic according to configured rules.
Next-Generation Firewall: a firewall with capabilities such as application awareness, deeper inspection, and integrated threat controls.
Web Application Firewall: filters HTTP/HTTPS traffic to protect web applications.

course.learn: Firewalls can filter at different layers and may specialize in different traffic. Traditional firewalls focus on network/transport rules; WAFs protect web applications; UTM and NGFW platforms combine broader capabilities.
course.why: Choosing the wrong firewall type can leave the actual attack layer uninspected.
course.example: A company keeps a network firewall at the Internet edge and adds a WAF in front of a public web application for HTTP-specific threats.
course.exam: Match tool to layer: WAF = web app, NGFW = application-aware firewall, UTM = multiple integrated security services.

defs: A control that permits or blocks network traffic according to configured rules.
Web Application Firewall: filters HTTP/HTTPS traffic to protect web applications.

course.learn: A Web Application Firewall (WAF) inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic with awareness of web requests and application-layer attacks.
course.why: Traditional network filtering may allow TCP 443 while malicious content still passes inside the permitted connection.
course.example: A WAF blocks a request containing a known SQL-injection pattern before it reaches the web application.
course.exam: WAF = web/application-layer protection. It complements secure coding; it is not a substitute for fixing the application.

breakdown.explanation: Application monitoring measures application behavior, performance, errors, and security events. APM focuses on health/performance, while a WAF inspects and protects web requests.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: A control that permits or blocks network traffic according to configured rules.
Next-Generation Firewall: a firewall with capabilities such as application awareness, deeper inspection, and integrated threat controls.

course.learn: A Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) extends traditional IP/port filtering with application awareness, deep inspection, identity context, and often integrated threat prevention.
course.why: Applications can share ports, so Layer-7 awareness lets policy describe the actual application rather than only TCP/UDP numbers.
course.example: A firewall allows Microsoft 365 traffic on HTTPS but blocks an unauthorized file-sharing application using the same port.
course.exam: Application-aware firewall = NGFW. Traditional Layer-4 filtering mainly uses addresses, protocols, and ports.

course.learn: Layer-4 filtering makes decisions using transport/network information such as IP addresses, protocols, and TCP/UDP ports. Layer-7 filtering understands application protocols and content.
course.why: Deeper inspection enables more precise policy but costs more processing and may require decryption visibility.
course.example: A Layer-4 rule allows TCP 443; a Layer-7 rule permits approved SaaS traffic while blocking another application that also uses HTTPS.
